tagline: Lake causeways follow a valley where two towns were submerged
intro: The Tappan-Moravian Trail winds for 55 miles through eastern Ohio’s rural lake country, passing Tappan Lake and circling Clendening Lake. Ohio’s byways program presents the scenic route as a journey through two lake regions and country traveled by the Delaware and Wyandot tribes. Along Tappan Lake, US 250 follows the water for several miles on causeways.

Those causeways date to the lake’s construction in the 1930s. When the reservoir was completed in 1938, it inundated the community of Tappan, whose name the lake carries. Laceyville also lies beneath the water.

The lake-road section follows US 250 between Dennison and Cadiz. In the northern villages, Jewett marks an end of the Conotton Creek rail trail. Germano stands on State Routes 9 and 646; at New Rumley, the Custer birthplace memorial stands beside Route 646.

moments.title: Tappan Dam
moments.text: Completion of the reservoir in 1938 inundated Tappan; Laceyville also lies beneath the lake. The road belongs to that same transformation: US 250 follows the shoreline on causeways built during the lake’s construction in the 1930s. The reservoir occupies 2,350 acres within the Muskingum Watershed Conservancy District.
moments.notice: US 250 follows the lake on causeways built in the 1930s.

moments.title: Jewett
moments.text: Streetcars built in Jewett traveled far beyond this Ohio village. The Jewett Car Company manufactured them here from 1894 until 1904, when it moved to Newark, Ohio. The village itself had changed names, from Fairview to Jewett, honoring railroad official T. M. Jewett. Fairview was platted in 1851; the streetcar factory arrived more than four decades after that initial town layout. A different use of a rail corridor now reaches the village: Jewett is an endpoint of the paved Conotton Creek Trail, a former railway route used for walking and cycling along the creek.

moments.title: New Rumley
moments.text: Only foundations remain of the house where George Armstrong Custer was born in New Rumley. Erwin Frey’s memorial stands on the community’s west side beside State Route 646. It combines a statue with an exhibit pavilion containing information on Custer’s life. The birthplace site also has a museum operated by the Custer Memorial Association.
moments.notice: The birthplace survives as foundations beside the statue and exhibit pavilion.
